Time, Distance, Shielding, the Inverse Square Law, and ALARA in Practice

Unit 2: Radiation, Magnetic, and Facility Safety. Lesson 7 of 60 in CRES Academy.

Three rules protect everyone in the room, and one formula decides how well. This lesson is the arithmetic a technician is expected to do standing in the suite.

The three cardinal rules

  • Time: dose is proportional to beam-on time, so minimize time; pulsed fluoroscopy and short exposures cut it directly.
  • Distance: maximize distance, because it is the strongest control there is and it is free. One step back beats any apron.
  • Shielding: aprons, thyroid shields, mobile barriers, the control booth, and the lead in the walls, used after time and distance rather than instead of them.

The inverse square law

Intensity falls with the square of the distance, because the same photons spread over a larger area.

I1 / I2 = (d2 / d1) squared

Example 1: 16 mGy/h at 1 m. At 2 m: 16 x (1/2) squared = 4 mGy/h. Double the distance, one quarter the rate.
Example 2: 2 mGy/h at 2 m. At 1 m: 2 x (2/1) squared = 8 mGy/h. Half the distance, four times the rate.

The same law runs the other way in fluoroscopy: halving the source-to-skin distance from 40 cm to 20 cm raises entrance exposure about four times, which is why the spacer that enforces the minimum distance is never removed.

ALARA as a program, not a slogan

ALARA means as low as reasonably achievable, and an inspector looks for it in three forms: written policies that set it as the facility's goal, procedures that implement it (protocols by size, pediatric technique charts, pulsed defaults, collimation rules), and physical actions you can point to (shields on the walls, barriers in the room, apparel inspected, interlocks proved). Your part is the physical and the recorded part: a collimator lamp that works, a pulsed mode that still defaults correctly after a software update, and a service record that says you verified it. What the program is chasing is dose reduction, and what it is removing is every unnecessary exposure: a field wider than the anatomy, a repeat, a magnification mode left engaged, a study already done down the hall.

Fluoroscopy practice

  • Use pulsed mode rather than continuous, and let last-image hold replace a second look.
  • Collimate to the anatomy; magnification modes raise dose rate, so they are used deliberately and briefly.
  • The cumulative timer gives an audible signal at 5 minutes of beam-on time, and beam-on time is recorded for the exam.
  • Stand on the image-receptor side of the patient rather than the tube side, behind the drape and the table shield, and step back whenever you are not needed at the table.

Pediatric and pregnancy practice

Ask about pregnancy, let the patient declare it, and once declared the monthly embryo or fetus limit of 0.5 mSv applies. Shield what is not being imaged, collimate tightly, use the lowest technique that answers the question, immobilize rather than accept motion, and avoid the repeat entirely, because a repeat doubles the dose of that image. Children are more radiosensitive because dividing cells are the most sensitive cells there are.

Repeat analysis is a dose program

Counting repeats by room, by reason, and by technologist finds the uncollimated room, the drifting detector, the miscalibrated automatic exposure control, and the training gap. It belongs in your quality control data because every repeat is a dose nobody needed to give.

Exam tip: distance beats everything, and the inverse square law is squared both ways: double it for a quarter, halve it for four times. The fluoroscopic timer signals at 5 minutes. ALARA shows up as policy, procedure, and physical action, and a repeat is a dose event.
Remember
Time, distance, and shielding in that order of power; intensity follows I1 over I2 equals d2 over d1 squared, so doubling the distance quarters the rate and halving it quadruples it; ALARA has to show as policy, procedure, and physical action; pulsed mode, last-image hold, collimation, the 5-minute timer, and standing on the receptor side protect the operator; and pregnancy means declare, shield, collimate, lowest technique, and no repeats against a 0.5 mSv monthly limit.
Deeper explanation

Time, Distance, Shielding, the Inverse Square Law, and ALARA in Practice, explained slowly

Three rules, in order of power

Time, distance, and shielding are listed in that order out of habit, but ranked by how much good they do per unit of effort, distance wins by a wide margin, then time, then shielding. The reason is arithmetic: time and shielding are linear or exponential improvements you have to carry or schedule, while distance is squared and free.

The inverse square law, worked three ways

I1 / I2 = (d2 / d1) squared      intensity falls with the square of the distance

1. 16 mGy/h at 1 m. At 2 m?        16 x (1/2) squared = 4 mGy/h
2. 2 mGy/h at 2 m. At 1 m?         2 x (2/1) squared = 8 mGy/h
3. 100 microGy/h at 1 m. At 4 m?   100 / 16 = 6.25 microGy/h
4. Where is the rate 1/9 of what    at 3 x the distance
   it is at 1 m?

Two habits make these free marks. First, write down which way the distance is going before you square anything: moving away divides, moving closer multiplies. Second, remember that the ratio is distance from the source, which in scatter work is the patient, not the tube. The same law explains the fluoroscopic rule: cutting source-to-skin distance from 40 cm to 20 cm raises entrance exposure about four times, which is the reason the spacer enforcing the minimum distance is a federal requirement and not an accessory.

ALARA as something an inspector can see

ALARA is a program with three visible layers.

Layer                 What it looks like                     Who owns it
Policy                a written statement that the facility   administration, through the
                      keeps dose as low as reasonably         radiation safety committee
                      achievable, with investigation levels
Procedure             protocols by patient size, pediatric    radiology, the physicist
                      technique charts, pulsed defaults,
                      collimation and shielding rules,
                      repeat analysis
Physical action       working collimator lamps, accurate      you
                      light fields, inspected apparel,
                      proved interlocks, calibrated output,
                      barriers and shields in place

Your layer is the one with measurements attached, which is also the layer a surveyor can verify fastest. A pulsed fluoroscopy default that silently reverted after a software update is an ALARA failure with your name on the last service record.

Fluoroscopy practice, in dose order

  • Pulsed instead of continuous is the largest saving available to the operator, and last-image hold removes the reflex second look.
  • Collimate, because it reduces both the patient's irradiated volume and the scatter that reaches everyone else.
  • Magnification raises dose rate, so it is used briefly and deliberately.
  • Keep the receptor close to the patient and the tube far from the skin; the automatic brightness control will otherwise raise output to defend image brightness.
  • The cumulative timer gives an audible signal at 5 minutes of beam-on time, and beam-on time is recorded for the exam.
  • Stand on the receptor side rather than the tube side, use the drape and the table shield, and step back when you are not needed at the table.

Pediatric and pregnancy practice

Ask; let the patient declare; once declared, the 0.5 mSv monthly embryo or fetus limit applies and the exam is justified, deferred, or done with the lowest technique that answers the question. Shield what is not being imaged, collimate tightly, immobilize rather than accept motion, and treat a repeat as a dose event rather than an inconvenience: a repeated image is exactly twice the dose of a single one. Children are more radiosensitive because dividing cells are the most sensitive cells there are, and they have more years ahead in which a late effect can appear.

Repeat analysis belongs to you too

Counting repeats by room, by reason, and by operator is a dose program and a diagnostic tool at once. A room with a rising repeat rate for positioning has a lamp, a light field, or a detent problem. A rising rate for exposure has an automatic exposure control, a detector calibration, or a technique chart problem. Bring the data to the committee rather than waiting for a complaint.

What to memorize

  • Time, distance, shielding; distance is squared and therefore strongest.
  • I1 / I2 = (d2 / d1) squared. Double the distance for a quarter of the rate; halve it for four times.
  • Halving source-to-skin distance from 40 cm to 20 cm roughly quadruples entrance exposure.
  • ALARA is policy, procedure, and physical action. Fluoroscopic timer at 5 minutes. Declared pregnancy 0.5 mSv per month.
